To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

liver transplantation is indicated in patients with unresected malignant tumours of liver parenchyma and bile ducts, provided that the tumour is small and the underlying liver disease is cirrhosis, or in the case of liver metastases from endocrine tumours.

the indication for transplantation should be restricted to early stage hepatobiliary malignancies and that resection of these lesions should be considered as an alternative to transplantation, especially in the presence of underlying cirrhosis.

liver transplantation is indicated in patients with early stage hepatocellar carcinoma with underlying cirhosis, and in patients with unresected hepatobiliary malignancies with predictable likelihood for a long-term survival after transplantation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the results of liver transplantation for hepatocellular carcinoma compare with resection of the same tumours.
the question of which patients with malignant hepatobiliary tumours might be cured by liver transplantation and which patients might be better served by other therapeutic modalities.
the question whether liver transplantation is a suitable treatment for unresectable hepatocarcinoma and other malignant tumours of liver and biliary tract.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
transplantation is not the treatment of choice for unresectable malignant tumours of liver.
liver transplantation for unresectable malignant tumours of liver is not justified.
liver transplantation is not the ideal treatment for all patients with malignant tumours of liver.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the indication for liver transplantation in malignant tumours of liver should be restricted to early stage hepatobiliary carcinoma and liver metastases from non-endocrine tumours.
liver transplantation is an effective treatment for selected patients with unresected malignant hepatobiliary tumours.
transplantation should be restricted to early stage hepatobiliary malignancies, but not be considered as a standard therapy for unresectable hepatocelluar carcinoma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the selection of patients for liver transplantation is crucial for the outcome of the procedure.
, for patients with hepatocellular carcinoma, the choice of treatment is not between transplantation or resection but between transplantation and no treatment.
the decision for liver transplantation in hepatocellular and bile duct carcinoma has to be made on the basis of tumour stage, the patient's general condition and the availability of a donor organ.
